Stochastic Subspace Descent Accelerated via Bi-fidelity Line Search

Nuojin Cheng nuojin.cheng@colorado.edu Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics Affiliation: University of Colorado Boulder    Alireza Doostan alireza.doostan@colorado.edu Affiliation: Smead Aerospace Engineering Sciences Department Affiliation: University of Colorado Boulder    Stephen Becker stephen.becker@colorado.edu Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics Affiliation: University of Colorado Boulder
Abstract

Efficient optimization remains a fundamental challenge across numerous scientific and engineering domains, especially when objective function and gradient evaluations are computationally expensive. While zeroth-order optimization methods offer effective approaches when gradients are inaccessible, their practical performance can be limited by the high cost associated with function queries. This work introduces the bi-fidelity stochastic subspace descent (BF-SSD) algorithm, a novel zeroth-order optimization method designed to reduce this computational burden. BF-SSD leverages a bi-fidelity framework, constructing a surrogate model from a combination of computationally inexpensive low-fidelity (LF) and accurate high-fidelity (HF) function evaluations. This surrogate model facilitates an efficient backtracking line search for step size selection, for which we provide theoretical convergence guarantees under standard assumptions. We perform a comprehensive empirical evaluation of BF-SSD across four distinct problems: a synthetic optimization benchmark, dual-form kernel ridge regression, black-box adversarial attacks on machine learning models, and transformer-based black-box language model fine-tuning. Numerical results demonstrate that BF-SSD consistently achieves superior optimization performance while requiring significantly fewer HF function evaluations compared to relevant baseline methods. This study highlights the efficacy of integrating bi-fidelity strategies within zeroth-order optimization, positioning BF-SSD as a promising and computationally efficient approach for tackling large-scale, high-dimensional problems encountered in various real-world applications.

1 Introduction

In this work, we are interested in the unconstrained optimization problem

𝒙∗∈arg​min𝐱∈ℝD⁡f​(𝐱),\bm{x}^{\ast}\in\argmin_{\bm{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D}}f(\bm{x}), (1.1)

where the objective function f:ℝD→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{D}\to\mathbb{R} is assumed to be L-smooth (i.e., its gradient ∇f\nabla f is L-Lipschitz continuous). Crucially, we operate in a black-box setting where direct access to the gradient ∇f\nabla f is unavailable or computationally infeasible to obtain with low complexity (e.g., via closed-form expressions or automatic differentiation), thereby precluding the direct application of standard first-order or higher-order optimization techniques. Furthermore, we focus on high-dimensional scenarios where D is large (e.g., D≳100D\gtrsim 100), posing significant challenges related to computational cost and scalability for many traditional derivative-free optimization methods.

The primary focus of this work is on selecting an appropriate step size (a.k.a learning rate) αk>0\alpha_{k}>0 for iterative descent schemes of the form:

𝒙k+1=𝒙k−αk​𝒗k,\bm{x}_{k+1}=\bm{x}_{k}-\alpha_{k}\bm{v}_{k}, (1.2)

where 𝒗k∈ℝD\bm{v}_{k}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D} represents an estimate of the true gradient ∇f​(𝒙k)\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}) or another suitable descent direction at iteration kk. Selecting an appropriate step size αk\alpha_{k} dynamically can significantly improve the convergence performance of the optimization process. This is illustrated in Figure 1, where an example function is optimized using different methods with and without a step size tuning scheme. However, common practices in machine learning often involve either using a fixed step size throughout the optimization or employing a predefined adaptive step size scheduling, e.g., Duchi et al. (2011). While convenient to implement, these approaches often neglect the intrinsic local geometry and characteristics of the objective function.

In contrast, classical line search methods, including exact line search and backtracking algorithms, typically yield better step sizes by incorporating information from additional objective function evaluations within each iteration. However, the cost of these additional evaluations can render such methods impractical, particularly when the computational budget is limited – a common situation in black-box optimization or when evaluating ff (or its gradients) is expensive.

To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach to tune the step size by leveraging multi-fidelity evaluations of the objective function. Here, multi-fidelity modeling involves utilizing two or more levels of objective function representations: the high-fidelity (HF) objective ff, which provides accurate but expensive evaluations, and one or more low-fidelity (LF) objectives that serve as cheaper, albeit less accurate, approximations of ff. We emphasize that this multi-fidelity setup (often bi-fidelity, involving one HF and one LF model) does not necessarily need to originate from the problem’s inherent structure. Even for a problem initially defined with a single fidelity, a practitioner can potentially construct a multi-fidelity extension (e.g., by creating simplified surrogate models) to accelerate the optimization procedure, particularly through more informed step size selection.

For simplicity, we focus on the bi-fidelity case, where only two fidelity levels are considered. The HF objective, fHFf^{\textup{HF}}, is treated as the ground-truth objective function, so we treat fHFf^{\textup{HF}} and the ff from Equation (1.1) synonymously. We construct simple bi-fidelity surrogates after obtaining the gradient estimation 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k}. Specifically, given the LF objective fLF:ℝD→ℝf^{\textup{LF}}:{\mathbb{R}}^{D}\to{\mathbb{R}}, the current position 𝒙k\bm{x}_{k}, 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k}, an initial step size αmax\alpha_{\textup{max}}, and a budget nkn_{k} for HF evaluations at this step, the local 1D surrogate of the HF objective φk​(α)≔fHF​(𝒙k−α​𝒗k):ℝ→ℝ\varphi_{k}(\alpha)\coloneqq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k}-\alpha\bm{v}_{k}):{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}} is constructed as

φ~k​(α,nk)=ρ​fLF​(𝒙k−α​𝒗k)+ψ~k​(α,nk),α∈[0,αmax].\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(\alpha;n_{k})=\rho f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x}_{k}-\alpha\bm{v}_{k})+\tilde{\psi}_{k}(\alpha;n_{k}),\quad\alpha\in[0,\alpha_{\textup{max}}]. (1.3)

Here, ρ\rho is a scalar, and ψ~k​(⋅,nk):ℝ→ℝ\tilde{\psi}_{k}(\cdot;n_{k}):{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}} is a piecewise linear function constructed using nkn_{k} HF evaluations. Once the surrogate φ~k\tilde{\varphi}_{k} is constructed, the step size is selected using backtracking line search by (approximately) solving

αk=arg​minα∈[0,αmax]⁡φ~k​(α,nk).\alpha_{k}=\argmin_{\alpha\in[0,\alpha_{\textup{max}}]}\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(\alpha;n_{k}). (1.4)

Assuming the scalar ρ\rho is properly chosen so that the difference

d⁡(𝒙)≔fHF​(𝒙)−ρ​fLF​(𝒙)d(\bm{x})\coloneqq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x})-\rho f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x}) (1.5)

is Lipschitz continuous, we show that the convergence of this descent method is guaranteed, and Kϵ=𝒪⁡(L/ϵ)K_{\epsilon}=\mathcal{O}(L/\epsilon) iterations are needed to ensure that mink⁡∥∇fHF​(𝒙k)∥2\min_{k}\lVert\nabla f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2} is ϵ\epsilon-small. Moreover, when the HF and LF functions are well-aligned, i.e., the Lipschitz constant WW of d⁡(𝒙)d(\bm{x}) is small, the required number of HF function evaluations Nϵ=𝒪⁡(W​L2/ϵ+D​L/ϵ)N_{\epsilon}=\mathcal{O}(WL^{2}/\epsilon+DL/\epsilon) is not large.

For implementation, we focus on high-dimensional zeroth-order optimization problems, using the stochastic subspace descent (SSD) method (Kozak et al., 2021) combined with the proposed step size tuning strategy, and call the resulting method bi-fidelity stochastic subspace descent (BF-SSD). BF-SSD demonstrates strong empirical performance across various tasks and holds great potential for future applications.

1.1 Related Work

Line Search for Optimization

Line search is a widely used method for determining step sizes in optimization algorithms. Line searches can be either exact, meaning that α\alpha is chosen to exactly or almost exactly minimize fHF​(𝒙k−α​𝒗k)f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k}-\alpha\bm{v}_{k}), or inexact. Exact line searches are computationally expensive, so other than in special cases, they are rarely used in practice. Common inexact line search methods include backtracking line search (Nocedal & Wright, 1999), the Polyak step size (Polyak, 1987), spectral methods such as (Barzilai & Borwein, 1988), and learning rate scheduling (Duchi et al., 2011). Among these, backtracking line search is particularly popular due to its simplicity and explainable design, often employing stopping criteria like the Armijo and Wolfe conditions (Nocedal & Wright, 1999). However, backtracking line search increases the overall computational costs considerably due to the numerous function evaluations required at each iteration. One way to mitigate this issue is by constructing surrogate models to guide step size selection. For example, Yue & Meerbergen (2013) and Grundvig (2023) used reduced-order models to approximate the objective function during line search, while Mahsereci & Hennig (2017) and Cartis & Scheinberg (2018) employed a probabilistic Gaussian model for step size selection. Paquette & Scheinberg (2020) provided a theoretical analysis of line search in stochastic optimization. A recent work by Nguyen et al. (2025) extends the backtracking line search framework to the stochastic ISTA/FISTA method. These approaches do not account for the multi-fidelity structure of objective functions, which is the focus of this work.

Derivative-Free and Zeroth-Order Optimization

Derivative-free optimization refers to a family of optimization techniques that rely solely on function evaluations, without requiring gradient information, to find the optimum of an objective function. This category includes methods such as Bayesian optimization (Shahriari et al., 2015), direct search (Kolda et al., 2003), trust region methods (Conn et al., 2000), genetic algorithms (Srinivas & Patnaik, 1994), and zeroth-order optimization (Liu et al., 2020). Among these, zeroth-order methods stand out for their scalability to high-dimensional problems and reliable convergence properties. Following Liu et al. (2020), we refer to zeroth-order algorithms as the type of algorithms that approximate gradients using finite difference techniques and subsequently apply strategies similar to first-order methods. These methods have shown great promise in various machine learning applications where objective functions are smooth but lack accessible or easy-to-compute derivatives. Recent advances include their use in solving black-box adversarial attacks (Chen et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2023) and fine-tuning large models, such as MeZO, S-MeZO, SubZO, etc. (Sun et al., 2022a; Sun et al., 2022b; Malladi et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), with minimal memory overhead. A recent work (Brilli et al., 2024) discloses the worst-case bound for derivative-free optimization with a line search-style method.

Randomized Zeroth-Order Optimization for High-Dimensional Problems

In high-dimensional zeroth-order optimization problems, estimating gradients via finite differences can be computationally prohibitive. To address this, randomized algorithms have been proposed to reduce the cost of gradient estimation. The simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) (Spall, 1992; Spall, 1998) uses Rademacher random vectors for gradient estimation, while Gaussian smoothing methods (Nesterov & Spokoiny, 2017) employ Gaussian random vectors. These algorithms typically provide gradient estimates projected onto one-dimensional subspaces. However, for certain problems, it is worth the increased number of function calls to improve gradient estimates. SSD (Kozak et al., 2021) explores this idea by projecting the gradient onto a random subspace of dimension ℓ\ell for any 1≤ℓ≤D1\leq\ell\leq D, providing a more generalized framework for randomized zeroth-order optimization.

Multi-Fidelity Modeling and Optimization

Multi-fidelity is a well-established concept in engineering and scientific computing for reducing computational costs. It has been widely applied across various domains, including aerodynamic design (Zhang et al., 2021), structural optimization (Ng & Willcox, 2014; De et al., 2020), data sampling (Cheng et al., 2024b), and uncertainty quantification (Peherstorfer et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2024a; De & Doostan, 2022; De et al., 2023; Cheng & Doostan, 2025). As one sub-branch, multi-fidelity optimization has been employed in hyperparameter tuning (Wu et al., 2020), accelerating Bayesian optimization (Kandasamy et al., 2016; Takeno et al., 2020), and reinforcement learning (Cutler et al., 2014) within machine learning. However, despite its relevance in settings where function evaluations are costly, its application in zeroth-order optimization remains largely unexplored (de Montbrun & Gerchinovitz, 2024) and has not been applied to any randomized zeroth-order method.

1.2 Contributions

In this work, we propose a multi-fidelity line search scheme. Unlike previous works that use static surrogate (reduced-order) models which do not change from iteration to iteration (Yue & Meerbergen, 2013; Grundvig, 2023) , our method constructs a temporary surrogate after the gradient is estimated. This allows us to focus on building a one-dimensional surrogate which is a much easier task than building an accurate DD-dimensional surrogate to ff. By leveraging a LF model, we construct a simple linear surrogate using a small number of HF evaluations, nkn_{k}. This surrogate facilitates the identification of an optimal step size, assuming certain conditions between the LF and HF models hold.

Specifically, this work makes the following contributions:

  1. 1.

    We develop the BF-SSD algorithm, a stochastic zeroth-order optimization method with a bi-fidelity line search that allows for choosing the approximation quality of the gradient by tuning ℓ\ell (reducing to deterministic gradient descent when ℓ=D\ell=D).

  2. 2.

    When the error of the gradient estimate is negligible (e.g., ℓ\ell is sufficiently large), we give specific conditions on the relation between the HF and LF functions that will guarantee convergence to a stationary point (or a global minimizer when ff is convex).

  3. 3.

    We highlight that many machine learning problems naturally have a corresponding LF model that can be used to construct a surrogate model, improving optimization efficiency. Despite its high potential, this strategy has not received sufficient attention in prior work.

  4. 4.

    We compare BF-SSD with other zeroth-order optimization methods on one synthetic function and the following three real-world applications:

    • •

      Kernel ridge regression with a Nyström-based LF approximation;

    • •

      Black-box image-based adversarial attacks with a LF model trained via knowledge distillation;

    • •

      Soft prompting of language models using a smaller training set to construct the bi-fidelity line search.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the proposed bi-fidelity line search method and provides convergence results. Section 3 details the implementation of the proposed method with SSD. Section 4 presents the experimental results, and Section 5 concludes the paper.

2 Line Search on Bi-fidelity Surrogate

In this section, we discuss the proposed algorithm and the main theoretical results delivered in this work. Unless specified, ∥⋅∥\lVert\cdot\rVert denotes the Euclidean norm for vectors and 2-norm for matrices. For simplicity and to keep our focus on the main contributions, in the proofs, we assume the gradient ∇fHF​(𝒙k)\nabla f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k}) can be accurately estimated by 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k}.

2.1 Algorithm

First, we define the algorithm, which consists of three steps for each iteration kk:

  1. 1.

    Given the current position 𝒙k∈ℝD\bm{x}_{k}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D}, gradient 𝒗k∈ℝD\bm{v}_{k}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D}, and initial step size αmax∈ℝ\alpha_{\textup{max}}\in{\mathbb{R}}, sample nkn_{k} equi-spaced HF evaluations in [0,αmax][0,\alpha_{\textup{max}}] and build the surrogate φ~k:ℝ→ℝ\tilde{\varphi}_{k}:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}} following Equation (1.3) (see Algo. 1 for details);

  2. 2.

    Given Armijo condition parameters c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1), β≤1/2\beta\leq 1/2, and initial step size αmax≥c/(L+c​L)\alpha_{\textup{max}}\geq c/(L+cL), conduct bi-fidelity adjusted Armijo backtracking so that

    αk\displaystyle\alpha_{k} =maxm∈ℕ⁡cm​αmax\displaystyle=\max_{m\in\mathbb{N}}c^{m}\alpha_{\textup{max}} (2.1)
    s.t.φ~k​(cm​αmax,nk)\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(c^{m}\alpha_{\textup{max}};n_{k}) ≤fHF​(𝒙k)−β​cm​αmax​∥𝒗k∥2.\displaystyle\leq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})-\beta c^{m}\alpha_{\textup{max}}\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}.

    See Algo. 2 for details.

  3. 3.

    Evaluate fHFf^{\textup{HF}} at the new point and continue the iterations.

2.2 Convergence Results

For convergence, we make the following assumptions:

Assumption 2.1.

The objective function fHF:ℝD→ℝf^{\textup{HF}}:{\mathbb{R}}^{D}\to{\mathbb{R}} attains its minimum f∗f^{\ast} and ∇fHF\nabla f^{\textup{HF}} is LL-Lipschitz continuous; i.e., there exists L∈ℝL\in{\mathbb{R}} such that

∥∇fHF​(𝒙)−∇fHF​(𝒚)∥≤L⁡∥𝒙−𝒚∥,∀𝒙,𝒚∈ℝD.\lVert\nabla f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x})-\nabla f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{y})\rVert\leq L\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{y}\rVert,\quad\forall\bm{x},\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D}. (2.2)

Note that Assumption 2.1 is standard for analysis of zeroth- and first-order methods. The constant LL must be known to the algorithm since it is used to set αmax\alpha_{\textup{max}}.

Assumption 2.2.

The difference between fHFf^{\textup{HF}} and fLFf^{\textup{LF}} is assumed to be smooth with a bounded Lipschitz constant. Specifically, we assume there exists W,ρ∈ℝW,\rho\in{\mathbb{R}} such that

∥(fHF​(𝒙)−ρ​fLF​(𝒙))−(fHF​(𝒚)−ρ​fLF​(𝒚))∥≤W⁡∥𝒙−𝒚∥,∀𝒙,𝒚∈ℝD.\lVert\left(f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x})-\rho f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x})\right)-\left(f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{y})-\rho f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{y})\right)\rVert\leq W\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{y}\rVert,\quad\forall\bm{x},\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D}. (2.3)

The Assumption 2.2 allows for fLFf^{\textup{LF}} to be uncalibrated, meaning that we do not require fLF​(𝒙)≈fHF​(𝒙)f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x})\approx f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}) since discrepancies can be reduced by building the surrogate φ~k\tilde{\varphi}_{k}.

Assumption 2.3.

For each iteration kk, the surrogate must be accurate; i.e., it satisfies Equation (2.8). In particular, a sufficient condition is that the number of HF evaluations, nkn_{k}, for building the surrogate φ~k\tilde{\varphi}_{k} is such that

nk≥W​L​(1+c)​αmaxc​β​∥𝒗k∥2,i.e.,nk=Ω⁡(W⁡(αmax​L+1)∥𝒗k∥2).n_{k}\geq\frac{WL(1+c)\alpha_{\textup{max}}}{c\beta\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}},\quad\text{i.e.,}\quad n_{k}=\Omega\left(\frac{W(\alpha_{\textup{max}}L+1)}{\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}}\right). (2.4)

Using 𝒗k=∇f​(𝒙k)\bm{v}_{k}=\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}) and with the above assumptions satisfied and sufficiently large initial step size αmax≥c/(c​L+L)\alpha_{\textup{max}}\geq c/(cL+L), the designed bi-fidelity line search leads to the following result:

Theorem 2.4.

Given an initial point 𝐱0\bm{x}_{0}, the algorithm in Section 2.1 generates a sequence (𝐱k)(\bm{x}_{k}) such that

mink∈{0,…,K}⁡∥∇fHF​(𝒙k)∥2≤2​L​(1+c)​(fHF​(𝒙0)−f∗)(K+1)​c​β.\min_{k\in\{0,\dots,K\}}\lVert\nabla f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{2L(1+c)(f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{\ast})}{(K+1)c\beta}. (2.5)

That is to say, Kϵ=𝒪⁡(L/ϵ)K_{\epsilon}=\mathcal{O}(L/\epsilon) iterations are required to obtain mink≤Kϵ⁡∥∇fHF​(𝐱k)∥2≤ϵ\min_{k\leq K_{\epsilon}}\lVert\nabla f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2}\leq\epsilon.

Remark 2.5.

Theorem 2.4 holds when 𝒗k=∇f​(𝒙k)\bm{v}_{k}=\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}). The error in approximating ∇f​(𝒙k)\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}) using finite difference methods with 𝒪⁡(D)\mathcal{O}(D) samples is typically negligible in comparison to the optimization error (see Kozak et al. (2023) for a precise quantitative statement for the case of SSD). Hence, assuming we accurately estimate 𝒗k=∇f​(𝒙k)\bm{v}_{k}=\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}) with 𝒪⁡(D)\mathcal{O}(D) samples per step, a bound for the total number of HF evaluations for ϵ\epsilon-convergence of the algorithm in Section 2.1 is

Nϵ=∑k=1Kϵ(nk+𝒪⁡(D))=𝒪⁡(W​L2ϵ+D​Lϵ).N_{\epsilon}=\sum_{k=1}^{K_{\epsilon}}\left(n_{k}+\mathcal{O}(D)\right)=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{WL^{2}}{\epsilon}+\frac{DL}{\epsilon}\right). (2.6)

The result in Equation (2.6) suggests that the number of function evaluations for ϵ\epsilon-convergence for the proposed algorithm can be significantly reduced when WW is small.

Remark 2.6.

When using zeroth-order gradient descent, with the same assumption that we accurately estimate 𝒗k=∇f​(𝒙k)\bm{v}_{k}=\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}) with 𝒪⁡(D)\mathcal{O}(D) samples per step, a bound for the total number of HF evaluations for ϵ\epsilon-convergence is

Nϵ=∑k=1Kϵ(logc−1⁡(αmax​L)+𝒪⁡(D))=𝒪⁡(L​log⁡(L)ϵ+D​Lϵ).N_{\epsilon}=\sum_{k=1}^{K_{\epsilon}}\left(\log_{c^{-1}}(\alpha_{\textup{max}}L)+\mathcal{O}(D)\right)=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{L\log(\Lip)}{\epsilon}+\frac{DL}{\epsilon}\right). (2.7)

The proof of Remark 2.6 follows the convergence proof of gradient descent using backtracking line search. Comparing the results in Equations (2.6) and (2.7), we observe that the advantage of using our bi-fidelity surrogate depends on the value of WW. Notice that if WW is sufficiently small so that W​L2≤L​log⁡LWL^{2}\leq L\log L, then the worst-case bound of our method is better than that of the zeroth-order gradient descent. We emphasize that our convergence result in Equation (2.6) is loose, due to the global nature of the Assumption 2.2 and difficulty in precisely describing the quality of the LF function relative to its HF counterpart. Hence, we view our convergence analysis as a reassurance that the method does converge, and rely on numerical experiments to elucidate when the method improves over baseline methods.

2.3 Proof of Theorem 2.4

Before the proof, we first introduce the following lemma:

Lemma 2.7.

With Assumption 2.2 and Assumption 2.3 satisfied, for any α∈[0,αmax]\alpha\in[0,\alpha_{\textup{max}}], the 1D surrogate φ~k​(α)\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(\alpha) satisfies the following bound,

|φ~k​(α,nk)−φ⁡(α)|≤∥𝒗k∥22​min⁡{c(1+c)2​L,c​β(1+c)​L,β​αmax}=c​β​∥𝒗k∥22​(1+c)​L.\displaystyle\lvert\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(\alpha;n_{k})-\varphi(\alpha)\rvert\leq\frac{\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}}{2}\min\left\{\frac{c}{(1+c)^{2}L},\frac{c\beta}{(1+c)L},\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}}\right\}=\frac{c\beta\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}}{2(1+c)L}. (2.8)

The proof of Lemma 2.7 is in Appendix A. Following this lemma, the proof of Theorem 2.4 is given below.

Proof.

Given Lemma 2.7, we have

|fHF​(𝒙k+1)−φ~k​(αk,nk)|=|φ⁡(αk)−φ~k​(αk,nk)|≤∥𝒗k∥22​min⁡{c(1+c)2​L,c​β(1+c)​L,β​αmax}\lvert f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k+1})-\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(\alpha_{k};n_{k})\rvert=\lvert\varphi(\alpha_{k})-\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(\alpha_{k};n_{k})\rvert\leq\frac{\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}}{2}\min\left\{\frac{c}{(1+c)^{2}L},\frac{c\beta}{(1+c)L},\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}}\right\} (2.9)

and, using the standard descent lemma for LL-smooth functions (guaranteed by Assumption 2.1),

fHF​(𝒙k+1)≤fHF​(𝒙k)−αk​∥𝒗k∥2+αk2​L2​∥𝒗k∥2.f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k+1})\leq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})-\alpha_{k}\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}+\frac{\alpha_{k}^{2}L}{2}\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}. (2.10)

Therefore, using the triangle inequality, the surrogate φ~k\tilde{\varphi}_{k} is bounded as

φ~k​(αk,nk)\displaystyle\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(\alpha_{k};n_{k}) ≤fHF​(𝒙k+1)+|fHF​(𝒙k+1)−φ~k​(αk,nk)|\displaystyle\leq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k+1})+\lvert f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k+1})-\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(\alpha_{k};n_{k})\rvert
≤fHF​(𝒙k)+(−αk+αk2​L2+c2​(1+c)2​L)​∥𝒗k∥2.\displaystyle\leq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})+\left(-\alpha_{k}+\frac{\alpha_{k}^{2}L}{2}+\frac{c}{2(1+c)^{2}L}\right)\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}.

When the step size satisfies αk∈[c/(L+c​L),1/(L+c​L)]\alpha_{k}\in[c/(L+cL),1/(L+cL)], the quadratic inequality −αk+αk2L/2+c/(2(1+c)2L)≤−αk/2-\alpha_{k}+\alpha_{k}^{2}L/2+c/(2(1+c)^{2}L)\leq-\alpha_{k}/2 holds, along with the fact that β≤1/2\beta\leq 1/2, which implies the following bi-fidelity-adjusted Armijo condition

φ~k​(αk,nk)\displaystyle\tilde{\varphi}_{k}\left(\alpha_{k};n_{k}\right) ≤fHF​(𝒙k)+(−αk+αk2​L2+c2​(1+c)2​L)​∥𝒗k∥2\displaystyle\leq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})+\left(-\alpha_{k}+\frac{\alpha_{k}^{2}L}{2}+\frac{c}{2(1+c)^{2}L}\right)\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2} (2.11)
≤fHF​(𝒙k)−αk2​∥𝒗k∥2\displaystyle\leq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})-\frac{\alpha_{k}}{2}\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}
≤fHF​(𝒙k)−β​αk​∥𝒗k∥2.\displaystyle\leq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})-\beta\alpha_{k}\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}.

The last line in Equation (2.11) satisfies the bi-fidelity-adjusted Armijo condition in Equation (2.1). Therefore, the bi-fidelity backtracking either terminates immediately with αk=αmax\alpha_{k}=\alpha_{\textup{max}} or else αk≥c/(L+c​L)\alpha_{k}\geq c/(L+cL), and implies

φ~k​(αk,nk)≤fHF​(𝒙k)−β​∥𝒗k∥2​min⁡{c(1+c)​L,αmax}=fHF​(𝒙k)−β​c(1+c)​L​∥𝒗k∥2,\tilde{\varphi}_{k}\left(\alpha_{k};n_{k}\right)\leq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})-\beta\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}\min\left\{\frac{c}{(1+c)L},\alpha_{\textup{max}}\right\}=f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})-\frac{\beta c}{(1+c)L}\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}, (2.12)

where the last equality comes from αmax≥c/((1+c)​L)\alpha_{\textup{max}}\geq c/((1+c)L). Using |fHF​(𝒙k+1)−φ~k​(αk,nk)|≤β​c​∥𝒗k∥2/(2​(1+c)​L)\lvert f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k+1})-\tilde{\varphi}_{k}\left(\alpha_{k};n_{k}\right)\rvert\leq\beta c\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}/(2(1+c)L) (from Lemma 2.7) and Equation (2.12), we have

fHF​(𝒙k+1)\displaystyle f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k+1}) ≤φ~k​(αk,nk)+|fHF​(𝒙k+1)−φ~k​(αk,nk)|\displaystyle\leq\tilde{\varphi}_{k}\left(\alpha_{k};n_{k}\right)+\bigg\lvert f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k+1})-\tilde{\varphi}_{k}\left(\alpha_{k};n_{k}\right)\bigg\rvert (2.13)
≤φ~k​(αk,nk)+β​c​∥𝒗k∥22​(1+c)​L\displaystyle\leq\tilde{\varphi}_{k}\left(\alpha_{k};n_{k}\right)+\frac{\beta c\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}}{2(1+c)L}
≤fHF​(𝒙k)−β​c​∥𝒗k∥22​(1+c)​L.\displaystyle\leq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})-\frac{\beta c\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}}{2(1+c)L}.

Equation (2.13) leads to the telescopic series

β​c2​(1+c)​L​∑k=0K∥𝒗k∥2\displaystyle\frac{\beta c}{2(1+c)L}\sum_{k=0}^{K}\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2} ≤∑k=0K(fHF​(𝒙k)−fHF​(𝒙k+1))\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{K}\left(f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})-f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k+1})\right) (2.14)
=fHF​(𝒙0)−fHF​(𝒙K+1)≤fHF​(𝒙0)−f∗.\displaystyle=f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{K+1})\leq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*}.

Hence,

(K+1)​mink∈{0,…,K}​∥𝒗k∥2\displaystyle(K+1)\min_{k\in\{0,\dots,K\}}\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2} ≤(β​c2​(1+c)​L)−1​(fHF​(𝒙0)−f∗)\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{\beta c}{2(1+c)L}\right)^{-1}(f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*}) (2.15)
=2​(1+c)​Lβ​c​(fHF​(𝒙0)−f∗).\displaystyle=\frac{2(1+c)L}{\beta c}\left(f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*}\right).

To guarantee mink≤Kϵ⁡∥∇fHF​(𝒙k)∥2≤ϵ\min_{k\leq K_{\epsilon}}\lVert\nabla f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2}\leq\epsilon, the value of KϵK_{\epsilon} should be

Kϵ≥2​(fHF​(𝒙0)−f∗)​(1+c)​Lβ​c​ϵ=𝒪⁡(Lϵ).K_{\epsilon}\geq\frac{2(f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*})(1+c)L}{\beta c\epsilon}=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{L}{\epsilon}\right). (2.16)

Remark 2.8.

Even if fHFf^{\textup{HF}} is non-convex, Equation (2.13) implies that the method is a descent method, meaning fHF​(𝒙k+1)≤fHF​(𝒙k)f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k+1})\leq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k}). Hence, after KK iterations, it is natural to use 𝒙K\bm{x}_{K} as the output. This descent property is not enjoyed by other methods, such as subgradient descent, stochastic gradient descent, or Polyak step size gradient descent.

Remark 2.9.

If fHFf^{\textup{HF}} is convex, then Theorem 2.4 implies convergence to a global minimizer. Or, if fHFf^{\textup{HF}} satisfies the Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality with parameter μ\mu (which includes some non-convex functions, as well as all strongly convex functions), then Theorem 2.4 in conjunction with the descent property implies fHF​(𝒙K)−f∗≤L⁡(1+c)(K+1)​μ​c​β​(fHF​(𝒙0)−f∗)f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{K})-f^{\ast}\leq\frac{L(1+c)}{(K+1)\mu c\beta}(f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{\ast}), cf. Karimi et al. (2016).

2.4 Examples of Possible Low-Fidelity Functions

In practice, the LF function fLFf^{\textup{LF}} can be constructed in various ways. The most straightforward approach is when a multi-fidelity structure is intrinsically present in the problem. For example, in Cheng et al. (2024a, Section 5.1), the LF model is the exact solution to a simplified physical model that can be simulated with negligible cost, while the intended HF objective relies on relatively expensive finite element simulations. In most machine learning problems, the LF model is not explicitly given, making its construction necessary. In this section, we discuss multiple approaches for building the LF model and the associated upper bound on WW.

Affine Bi-Fidelity Relationship

The most ideal case occurs when the HF model is an affine transformation of the LF model, i.e., fHF​(𝒙)=ρ​fLF​(𝒙)+cf^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x})=\rho f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x})+c. In this case, the Lipschitz constant WW, as defined in Assumption 2.2, is zero, and the number of function evaluations required for convergence is proportional to the number of iterations, as nk=1n_{k}=1 is sufficient.

Quadratic Objective with Low-Rank LF Approximation

Consider the case where the objective is quadratic with a positive semi-definite matrix 𝑨∈ℝD×D\bm{A}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D\times D} and denote its rank-rr approximation 𝑨~∈ℝD×D\widetilde{\bm{A}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D\times D}, and assume that rank​(𝑨)≫rank​(𝑨~)\textup{rank}(\bm{A})\gg\textup{rank}(\widetilde{\bm{A}}). The HF objective is fHF​(𝒙)=12​⟨𝒙,𝑨​𝒙⟩+⟨𝒙,𝒂⟩f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{2}\langle\bm{x},\bm{A}\bm{x}\rangle+\langle\bm{x},\bm{a}\rangle for 𝒙∈𝒳\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}, where ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle denotes the Euclidean inner-product, and the LF objective is fLF​(𝒙)=12​⟨𝒙,𝑨~​𝒙⟩+⟨𝒙,𝒂⟩f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{2}\langle\bm{x},\tilde{\bm{A}}\bm{x}\rangle+\langle\bm{x},\bm{a}\rangle. Assuming the input space 𝒳\mathcal{X} is bounded by a unit ball with radius RR, the Lipschitz constant WW is upper bounded as

W≤sup𝒙∥∇fHF​(𝒙)−∇fLF​(𝒙)∥=sup𝒙∥𝑨−𝑨~∥⋅∥𝒙∥≤λr+1​R,W\leq\sup_{\bm{x}}\lVert\nabla f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x})-\nabla f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x})\rVert=\sup_{\bm{x}}\lVert\bm{A}-\tilde{\bm{A}}\rVert\cdot\lVert\bm{x}\rVert\leq\lambda_{r+1}R, (2.17)

where λr+1\lambda_{r+1} is the (r+1)(r+1)-th largest eigenvalue of 𝑨\bm{A}. The empirical problems in Section 4.1 and Section 4.2.1 fall into this category.

Full-Batch HF and Mini-Batch LF Objectives

In many machine learning settings, the objective function is expressed as a sum over a large number of terms, each corresponding to the evaluation of a loss function on an individual data sample. In this case, a natural choice for the LF objective is the summation over a smaller subset of the data. Specifically, assuming that the HF objective sums over datapoints i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n and (without loss of generality, i.e., by relabeling) the LF objective sums over datapoints i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r for r≪nr\ll n, the HF objective is fHF​(𝒙)=1n​∑i=1nfi​(𝒙)f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}(\bm{x}), and the LF objective is fLF​(𝒙)=1r​∑i=1rfi​(𝒙)f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{r}\sum_{i=1}^{r}f_{i}(\bm{x}). Using the triangle inequality, the Lipschitz constant WW is upper bounded as

W≤sup𝒙‖1n​∑i=1n∇fi​(𝒙)−1r​∑i=1r∇fi​(𝒙)‖≤n−rn​(max1≤i≤r⁡‖∇fi​(𝒙)‖+max1≤i≤n⁡‖∇fi​(𝒙)‖).W\leq\sup_{\bm{x}}\left\lVert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\nabla f_{i}(\bm{x})-\frac{1}{r}\sum_{i=1}^{r}\nabla f_{i}(\bm{x})\right\rVert\leq\frac{n-r}{n}\left(\max_{1\leq i\leq r}\|\nabla f_{i}(\bm{x})\|+\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\|\nabla f_{i}(\bm{x})\|\right). (2.18)

The terms ‖∇fi​(𝒙)‖\|\nabla f_{i}(\bm{x})\| are bounded if each fif_{i} is Lipschitz, or equivalently, if fif_{i} is continuous and 𝒙\bm{x} is constrained to a compact set. An empirical problem with this setting is presented in Section 4.2.3. Our analysis is deterministic, so WW is a worst-case bound, but if rr is large and the LF subsamples are chosen uniformly at random, it would be reasonable to expect that, due to the law of large numbers, the average case behavior is significantly better than our bound.

Generic Case

Finally, we consider the most general case, without assuming specific relationships between the HF and LF objectives. By assuming the Lipschitz continuity of both the HF and LF objectives, WW can be bounded as

W=∥fHF​(𝒙)−ρ​fLF​(𝒙)∥L≤∥fHF​(𝒙)∥L+|ρ|⋅∥fLF​(𝒙)∥L,W=\lVert f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x})-\rho f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x})\rVert_{L}\leq\lVert f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x})\rVert_{L}+\lvert\rho\rvert\cdot\lVert f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x})\rVert_{L}, (2.19)

for any choice of ρ\rho, where ∥⋅∥L\lVert\cdot\rVert_{L} denotes the Lipschitz constant. The proportionality ρ\rho should not be chosen to minimize this bound (since that leads to ρ=0\rho=0) but can instead be chosen by any heuristic, such as the one used in control variate techniques (Gorodetsky et al., 2020) where ρ=−c^/v^\rho=-\hat{c}/\hat{v} where c^\hat{c} is an estimate of the covariance between fHFf^{\textup{HF}} and fLFf^{\textup{LF}}, and v^\hat{v} is an estimate of the variance of fHFf^{\textup{HF}}.

3 Bi-Fidelity Line Search with Stochastic Subspace Descent

In this manuscript, we focus on zeroth-order optimization, utilizing stochastic subspace descent (SSD) as the implementation method. Following the algorithmic steps introduced in Section 2.1, combined with SSD, the entire process is divided into three main (iteratively implemented) components: gradient estimation to construct 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k}, bi-fidelity surrogate construction, and Armijo backtracking on the surrogate.

Gradient Estimation

SSD employs a random projection matrix 𝑷k∈ℝD×ℓ\bm{P}_{k}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D\times\ell} with ℓ≪D\ell\ll D. The random matrix 𝑷k\bm{P}_{k} satisfies the properties 𝔼⁡[𝑷k​𝑷k⊤]=𝑰D{\mathbb{E}}[\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{\top}]=\bm{I}_{D} and 𝑷k⊤​𝑷k=(D/ℓ)​𝑰ℓ\bm{P}_{k}^{\top}\bm{P}_{k}=(D/\ell)\bm{I}_{\ell}. A common choice for 𝑷k\bm{P}_{k} is based on the Haar measure, where 𝑷k\bm{P}_{k} is derived from the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization of a random Gaussian matrix. The gradient estimation is given by 𝒗k=𝑷k​𝒈k\bm{v}_{k}=\bm{P}_{k}\bm{g}_{k}, where 𝒈k\bm{g}_{k} is the finite difference estimator of the gradient:

𝒈k≔[fHF​(𝒙k+Δ​𝒑1)−fHF​(𝒙k)Δ,fHF​(𝒙k+Δ​𝒑2)−fHF​(𝒙k)Δ,…,fHF​(𝒙k+Δ​𝒑ℓ)−fHF​(𝒙k)Δ]⊤,\bm{g}_{k}\coloneqq\left[\frac{f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k}+\Delta\bm{p}_{1})-f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})}{\Delta},\frac{f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k}+\Delta\bm{p}_{2})-f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})}{\Delta},\ldots,\frac{f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k}+\Delta\bm{p}_{\ell})-f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})}{\Delta}\right]^{\top}, (3.1)

where Δ∈ℝ\Delta\in{\mathbb{R}} is a small step size and 𝒑i\bm{p}_{i} is the ii-th column of 𝑷k\bm{P}_{k}. Estimating 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k} using Equation (3.1) requires ℓ\ell function evaluations – a more accurate 𝒪⁡(Δ2)\mathcal{O}(\Delta^{2}) approximation is also possible at the cost of 2​ℓ2\ell function evaluations if more than 8 digits of precision are needed. Up to the finite-difference error, 𝒈k≈𝑷k⊤∇fHF(𝒙k)\bm{g}_{k}\approx\bm{P}_{k}^{\top}\nabla f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k}) so that 𝒗k≈𝑷k𝑷k⊤∇fHF(𝒙k)\bm{v}_{k}\approx\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{\top}\nabla f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k}), hence 𝔼⁡[𝒗k]≈∇fHF​(𝒙k)\mathbb{E}[\bm{v}_{k}]\approx\nabla f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k}). It is also possible to construct the same estimator without reference to the Haar measure by rewriting 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k} as 𝒗k=projcol​(𝑸k)​(∇fHF​(𝒙k))\bm{v}_{k}=\text{proj}_{\text{col}(\bm{Q}_{k})}(\nabla f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})) where 𝑸k∈ℝD×ℓ\bm{Q}_{k}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D\times\ell} is any random matrix with independent columns from an isotropic probability distribution (such as the standard normal).

Surrogate Construction

Given the estimated gradient 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k} and the current position 𝒙k\bm{x}_{k}, the goal of surrogate construction is to build φ~k\tilde{\varphi}_{k}, denoted as

φ~k​(α)≔ρ​fLF​(𝒙k+α​𝒗k)+ψ~k​(α).\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(\alpha)\coloneqq\rho f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x}_{k}+\alpha\bm{v}_{k})+\tilde{\psi}_{k}(\alpha). (3.2)

The analysis in Section 2 assumes that ρ\rho is known and fixed. However, in practice, ρ\rho is tuned for better performance. In our application, we set ρk=fHF​(𝒙k)/fLF​(𝒙k)\rho_{k}=f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{k})/f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x}_{k}). We model ψ~k\tilde{\psi}_{k} as a piecewise linear function using nkn_{k} additional HF evaluations at equispaced points {0,α~1,…,α~nk=αmax}\{0,\tilde{\alpha}_{1},\dots,\tilde{\alpha}_{n_{k}}=\alpha_{\textup{max}}\}. Specifically,

ψ~k(α)=h−αhψ(α~j−1)+αhψ(α~j),α∈[α~j−1,α~j],j=1,…,nk,\tilde{\psi}_{k}(\alpha)=\frac{h-\alpha}{h}\psi(\tilde{\alpha}_{j-1})+\frac{\alpha}{h}\psi(\tilde{\alpha}_{j}),\quad\alpha\in[\tilde{\alpha}_{j-1},\tilde{\alpha}_{j}],\quad j=1,\dots,n_{k}, (3.3)

where h=αmax/nkh=\alpha_{\textup{max}}/n_{k} and ψ⁡(α)=ϕ⁡(α)−fLF​(𝒙k−α​𝒗k)\psi(\alpha)=\phi(\alpha)-f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x}_{k}-\alpha\bm{v}_{k}). This piecewise linear interpolation is a simple, yet effective, approach for interpolating φ\varphi in 1D and satisfies the bounds in Lemma 2.7 given sufficient nkn_{k}. The detailed algorithm is presented in Algorithm 1.

Figure 2 illustrates the bi-fidelity backtracking line search process using the example problem in Section 4.2.1. The blue curve represents the bi-fidelity surrogate model φ~k\tilde{\varphi}_{k} approximating the HF function φ\varphi (red curve). Rather than performing the line search directly on the computationally expensive HF function (red dots), the method utilizes the surrogate φ~k\tilde{\varphi}_{k} to estimate an optimal step size. While this surrogate is an approximation and may require more surrogate function evaluations during the search itself, it substantially reduces the computational cost of line search. In this example, the cost is decreased from 4 HF function calls (for a direct search) to only 1 HF call (to build the surrogate) combined with 6 LF function calls.

Armijo Backtracking on the Surrogate

Based on the criteria in Equation (2.1), we set the maximum number of iterations for testing the Armijo condition to M∈ℕM\in\mathbb{N}. The detailed procedure is presented in Algorithm 2.

Convergence Analysis of SSD with Line Search

The convergence results of SSD with line search (on the exact φ⁡(α)\varphi(\alpha)) are presented in Appendix B, under three separate scenarios: strongly convex, convex, and non-convex. The proof shows that, in the SSD with line search setting, the value of β\beta can be set as ℓ/2​D\ell/2D.

The proposed bi-fidelity line search algorithm, combined with SSD, will be referred to as bi-fidelity SSD (BF-SSD), and is summarized in Algorithm 3. Our theory covers either ℓ=D\ell=D with bi-fidelity line search (Thm. 2.4) or 1≤ℓ≤D1\leq\ell\leq D with HF line search (Appendix B). Combining the two analyses is fairly complicated, and we defer it to a future study.

For practical purposes, since the parameters in Assumption 2.3 are often unknown, we set ρk\rho_{k} as described above and choose nk=1n_{k}=1 to minimize the cost of generating φ~k​(α)\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(\alpha). This choice also demonstrates excellent empirical performance across all HF and LF pairs we have examined.

4 Empirical Experiments

In this section, we evaluate the proposed BF-SSD Algorithm 3 on four distinct: one synthetic optimization problem discussed in Section 4.1 and three machine learning-related problems across diverse scenarios presented in Section 4.2. These include dual-form kernel ridge regression (Section 4.2.1), black-box adversarial attacks (Section 4.2.2), and transformer-based black-box language model fine-tuning (soft prompting) in Section 4.2.3. We demonstrate that the BF-SSD algorithm consistently outperforms competing methods. To illustrate these advantages, we compare BF-SSD against the following baseline algorithms:

  • •

    Gradient descent (GD): A zeroth-order gradient descent method, where the full-batch gradient is estimated using forward differences, and a fixed step size is used.

  • •

    Coordinate descent (CD): Iteratively and individually optimizes each coordinate using finite-difference estimated coordinate gradients.

  • •

    Stochastic subspace descent with fixed step size (FS-SSD): The standard stochastic subspace descent method, which samples subspaces from the Haar measure and uses a fixed step size.

  • •

    Simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA): A randomized optimization method using a Hadamard random variable to estimate the gradient, as proposed by Spall (1992) and with step sizes as described in Spall (1998); this is a time-tested, well-established zeroth-order method.

  • •

    Gaussian smoothing (GS): A method popularized by Nesterov & Spokoiny (2017), which is nearly equivalent to SSD with ℓ=1\ell=1, and uses a fixed step size.

  • •

    High-Fidelity stochastic subspace descent (HF-SSD): A single-fidelity SSD method that utilizes a high-fidelity function for backtracking line search, with its convergence analysis detailed in Appendix B.

  • •

    Variance-reduced stochastic subspace descent (VR-SSD): A variance-reduced version of the SSD method inspired by SVRG (Johnson & Zhang, 2013), as described in the technical report Kozak et al. (2019, Section 2.2) of the SSD authors.

  • •

    Bi-fidelity stochastic subspace descent (BF-SSD): The proposed method detailed in Section 3.

The performance of the optimizers is assessed based on the number of HF objective function evaluations required, accounting for LF calls (in terms of fractional equivalent HF function calls) as appropriate. 11 1 The code is available at https://github.com/CU-UQ/BF-Stochastic-Subspace-Descent/.

4.1 Synthetic Problem: Worst Function in the World

In this section, we investigate the performance of our proposed BF-SSD algorithm on the “worst function in the world” (Nesterov, 2013). With a fixed Lipschitz constant L>0L>0, the function is

f⁡(𝒙,r,L)=L⁡(x12+∑i=1r−1(xi−xi+1)2+xr28−x14)−L​r8​(r+1),f(\bm{x};r,L)=L\left(\frac{x_{1}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}(x_{i}-x_{i+1})^{2}+x_{r}^{2}}{8}-\frac{x_{1}}{4}\right)-\frac{Lr}{8(r+1)}, (4.1)

where xix_{i} denotes the ithi^{\textup{th}} entry of the input 𝒙\bm{x} and r<Dr<D is a constant integer defining the intrinsic dimension of the problem. The function is convex with global minimum value 00. The Lipschitz constant of the gradient of this function is LL. Nesterov (2013) has shown that a wide range of iterative first-order methods perform poorly when minimizing f⁡(𝒙,r,L)f(\bm{x};r,L) with initial point 𝒙0=𝟎\bm{x}_{0}=\bm{0}.

We set the dimension D=1,000D=1,\!000, ℓ=20\ell=20, and L=20L=20. The intrinsic dimensions of the LF and HF functions are rHr_{H} and rLr_{L}, respectively. We choose rL≪rHr_{L}\ll r_{H} and assume the computational cost ratio between HF and LF evaluations is rH:rLr_{H}:r_{L}. For Gradient Descent, we choose the standard step size of 1/L=0.051/L=0.05, and for the GS and SSD-based methods, the step size is ℓ/(L​D)\ell/(LD). The backtracking parameter is β=ℓ/(2​D)\beta=\ell/(2D). The hyperparameter study is conducted according to different values of c∈{0.8,0.9,0.99}c\in\{0.8,0.9,0.99\} and ℓ∈{5,10,20}\ell\in\{5,10,20\}. All the experiments are repeated 10 times, with shaded regions denoting the worst and the best performance over 10 trials.

Figure 3 illustrates the performance of various optimizers across different values of ℓ\ell. Detailed results for ℓ=20\ell=20 and c=0.99c=0.99 at NN from 500 to 8,000 are presented in Table 1, while additional comparisons across different ℓ\ell and cc configurations are included in Table 4. These results show that BF-SSD consistently outperforms the other optimizers in most scenarios. For different SSD methods, the effect of ℓ\ell on the final performance varies. Large values of ℓ\ell improve the optimization results for FS-SSD and VR-SSD, while HF-SSD and BF-SSD prefer relatively smaller ℓ\ell, as highlighted in Table 2.

4.2 Zeroth-Order Optimization for Machine Learning Problems

Next, we contrast the BF-SSD optimization results against other competing zeroth-order methods. Besides showing the advantages of the BF-SSD, we also show that it is often convenient to design a cheap LF model in many machine learning problems that can be leveraged to accelerate the convergence.

4.2.1 Dual Form of Kernel Ridge Regression

Consider a kernel ridge regression problem as follows. By the representer theorem, given data {(𝒙i,yi)}i=1D\{(\bm{x}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{D} and a kernel function κ:ℝm~×ℝm~→ℝ\kappa:{\mathbb{R}}^{\tilde{m}}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{\tilde{m}}\to{\mathbb{R}}, the goal is to find the coefficients 𝜶~\tilde{\bm{\alpha}} such that

fpredict​(𝒙)=∑i=1Dα~i​k​(𝒙,𝒙i).f_{\textup{predict}}(\bm{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{D}\tilde{\alpha}_{i}k(\bm{x},\bm{x}_{i}). (4.2)

One way to compute the coefficients is to solve the dual form of the kernel ridge regression,

𝜶~∗=arg​min𝜶⁡𝜶T​𝐊​𝜶−2​⟨𝜶,𝐲⟩+λ​∥𝜶∥2,\tilde{\bm{\alpha}}^{*}=\argmin_{\bm{\alpha}}\bm{\alpha}^{T}\bm{K}\bm{\alpha}-2\langle\bm{\alpha},\bm{y}\rangle+\lambda\lVert\bm{\alpha}\rVert^{2}, (4.3)

where 𝑲\bm{K} is the kernel matrix with [𝑲]i,j=κ⁡(𝒙i,𝒙j)[\bm{K}]_{i,j}=\kappa(\bm{x}_{i},\bm{x}_{j}), [𝒚]i=yi[\bm{y}]_{i}=y_{i}, and λ\lambda is a positive scalar regularization parameter. The solution of Equation (4.3) can be explicitly represented as

𝜶~∗=(𝑲+λ​𝑰)−1​𝒚.\tilde{\bm{\alpha}}^{*}=(\bm{K}+\lambda\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{y}. (4.4)

However, solving the explicit solution involves inverting the matrix 𝑲+λ​𝑰\bm{K}+\lambda\bm{I}, which takes 𝒪⁡(D3)\mathcal{O}(D^{3}) and can be extremely expensive when DD is large. When DD is sufficiently large, evaluating the function in Equation (4.2) takes 𝒪⁡(D2)\mathcal{O}(D^{2}) and becomes expensive. Therefore, an alternative approach to solve this problem is to build a low-rank approximation (surrogate) of the kernel matrix 𝑲\bm{K}, which we adopt for evaluating the LF objective. To do this, we employ the Nyströem method, which finds a subset 𝒮⊂[1,…,D]\mathcal{S}\subset[1,\dots,D] with size l≪Dl\ll D and builds the kernel surrogate 𝑲~=𝑲[:,𝒮](𝑲[𝒮,𝒮])−1𝑲[𝒮,:]\tilde{\bm{K}}=\bm{K}[:,\mathcal{S}](\bm{K}[\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}])^{-1}\bm{K}[\mathcal{S},:]. By implementing the Nyströem method, the complexity of evaluating the objective function is reduced to 𝒪⁡(l​D)\mathcal{O}(lD). Therefore, the ratio of computational cost between HF and LF function evaluation is D/lD/l.

We pretend the problem in a black-box format, where access to the HF function is only available through an API, thus hiding 𝒚\bm{y} (and/or 𝑲\bm{K}) in Equation (4.3) and making derivative information inaccessible. In this case, we assume the values of 𝒚\bm{y} are unavailable for privacy reasons. For the regression data, we select the first D=1,000D=1,\!000 samples from the California housing dataset provided in the scikit-learn library (Pedregosa et al., 2011). A subset 𝒮\mathcal{S} with size l=10l=10 is randomly selected for the Nyströem approximation. We use a Gaussian (RBF) kernel with lengthscale 1.01.0 to generate the corresponding kernel matrix 𝑲\bm{K}. Figure 4 shows the decay of eigenvalues for 𝑲\bm{K}, with a rapid drop, especially within the first 100 eigenvalues, due to the Gaussian kernel’s properties. This fast decay motivates our focus on cases where the values of ℓ\ell are below 100. The starting point 𝒙0\bm{x}_{0} is set at the origin 𝟎\bm{0}.

The results of kernel ridge regression are shown in Figure 5, with values of cc chosen from 0.9 and 0.99, and the value of ℓ\ell is fixed as 100. According to these results, BF-SSD shows advantages over other methods except HF-SSD in Figure 5. When the backtracking factor cc decreases, the step sizes determined by the backtracking method become more conservative, leading to suboptimal results, especially for BF-SSD. We also implement different combinations of cc and ℓ\ell and collect the SSD performances in Table 3. The results suggest that BF-SSD outperforms other methods for most cases, and larger values of ℓ\ell and cc improve the performance of BF-SSD.

4.2.2 Black-box Adversarial Attack on MNIST

In practice, especially in explainable AI (XAI), researchers have found that many deep learning models are not robust to data noise. Specifically, if test data is contaminated by a small perturbation imperceptible to humans, many previously well-performing deep learning models fail to produce reasonable results (Goodfellow et al., 2014). Generating such biased noise to confuse a trained neural network model is usually referred to as “attack” in adversarially robust training. This need not be a “black hat” activity, as it can be used as part of hardening a system to prevent these attacks in the future.

There are primarily two types of attacks: one is a white-box attack, in which we have knowledge of the model and inject the adversarial noise to confuse the given model. The standard approach under this scenario is to generate the shift in pixel space based on the gradient of the objective function to maximize the loss. The other type of attack is called a black-box attack, in which one does not have knowledge of the trained model and would like to generate adversarial data from it. The black-box scenario is more difficult due to the missing knowledge, and one way to solve it is to treat this problem as a black box optimization. To generate an adversarial sample for a given data instance 𝒙†∈ℝD\bm{x}^{\dagger}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D}, with DD representing the number of pixels in the given image, a common formulation of the adversarial attack is to find a noise sample 𝒙∗\bm{x}^{*} solving

𝒙∗=argmax∥𝒙∥≤εℒ​(g⁡(𝒙+𝒙†),y†),\bm{x}^{*}=\argmax_{\lVert\bm{x}\rVert\leq\varepsilon}\mathcal{L}\left(g(\bm{x}+\bm{x}^{\dagger}),y^{\dagger}\right), (4.5)

where y†y^{\dagger} is the correct label of 𝒙†\bm{x}^{\dagger}, ℒ\mathcal{L} is the attack loss function, and gg represents the model for attack. Following the adversarial attack paradigm of Carlini & Wagner (2017) and its black-box extension (Chen et al., 2017), we use a soft version of the problem (4.5) as follows:

𝒙∗=arg​min𝐱−CE​(g⁡(𝐱+𝐱†),y†)+τ~​∥𝐱∥2,\bm{x}^{*}=\argmin_{\bm{x}}-\text{CE}\left(g(\bm{x}+\bm{x}^{\dagger}),{y^{\dagger}}\right)+\tilde{\tau}\lVert\bm{x}\rVert^{2}, (4.6)

where the cross entropy loss CE is assigned as the attack loss and g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) outputs the probabilities of different classes, usually using a softmax function for normalization. τ~\tilde{\tau} is a variable balancing the attack loss function CE and the attack norm. The optimization goal is to find a small shift 𝒙\bm{x} in pixel space so that the output results are greatly changed.

In this study, we utilized two convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures to model the HF and LF representations for classification tasks on the MNIST dataset with 60,00060,\!000 training data and 10,00010,\!000 testing data. The HF model was a deeper CNN consisting of two convolutional layers, the first with 32 filters and the second with 64 filters, both using 5×55\times 5 kernels, followed by ReLU activations and 2×22\times 2 max-pooling. The flattened output from the convolutional layers (7×7×647\times 7\times 64) was connected to a fully connected layer with 1024 neurons, followed by a 10-class output layer. In contrast, the LF model employed a simplified architecture with a single convolutional layer containing 2 filters and a 3×33\times 3 kernel, followed by ReLU activation and 2×22\times 2 max-pooling. The output (13×13×213\times 13\times 2) was flattened and passed through a fully connected layer with 16 neurons, leading to a 10-class output layer with log-softmax activation. The HF model was designed to provide high-capacity representations, while the LF model served as a lightweight alternative for computational efficiency. The LF model was trained using knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015), leveraging only 1000 training samples and 1000 evaluations of the HF function. Knowledge distillation is a technique where a smaller, simpler model (the student) learns to replicate the outputs of a larger, more complex model (the teacher), effectively transferring knowledge while reducing computational costs. The classification accuracy for the HF and LF CNNs are 99.02%99.02\% and 82.21%82.21\%, respectively. There are 27,56227,\!562 parameters for the LF CNN and 3,274,6343,\!274,\!634 parameters for the HF CNN. We estimate the ratio between HF and LF computational costs as 3274634/27562≈118.83274634/27562\approx 118.8. The images in MNIST dataset are 28×2828\times 28 with a single channel, hence the dimension is D=784D=784. The starting points are initialized as the origin point for all experiments.

Figure 6 illustrates the convergence of various zeroth-order methods on two test images. For the SSD methods (including the line search version), the parameters are set to ℓ=50\ell=50 and αmax=2.0\alpha_{\textup{max}}=2.0. Since BF-SSD uses 1,000 HF evaluations for knowledge distillation training, it begins at N=1,000N=1,\!000. The convergence results demonstrate that HF-SSD outperforms other methods in this task. Additionally, HF-SSD, BF-SSD, and SPSA exhibit clear advantages over other methods, underscoring the importance of tuning suitable step sizes for the optimization process.

In Figure 7, we present the adversarially attacked test images generated by different optimization approaches for N=2,000N=2,\!000, 5,0005,\!000, and 7,0007,\!000. For the first test image (a-f), only HF-SSD, BF-SSD, and SPSA successfully flip the output of the HF model under limited HF evaluations (N≤7,000N\leq 7,\!000). Similarly, for the second test image (g-l), HF-SSD, BF-SSD, SPSA, and VR-SSD succeed in flipping the HF model output. However, in both cases, we observe that HF-SSD (Figure 7 and Figure 7) and BF-SSD (Figure 7 and Figure 7) tend to blur the images more than SPSA (Figure 7 and Figure 7). This behavior may result from differences in sampling strategies, such as Haar measure sampling versus Hadamard sampling. From an adversarial attack perspective, a successful attack should flip the model’s output without excessively blurring the image. In this regard, SPSA outperforms HF-SSD and BF-SSD, although its loss function remains higher than that of the other methods. The reason for this observation requires further investigation but is out of the scope of this work.

4.2.3 Soft Prompting Black-box Language Model

Fine-tuning pre-trained models like BERT or GPT has become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing (NLP). These models, trained on massive corpora, achieve state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of downstream tasks when adapted using task-specific fine-tuning. However, traditional fine-tuning involves updating millions or even billions of parameters, making it computationally expensive and prone to overfitting, especially in low-resource settings. To address these challenges, soft prompting has emerged as a lightweight and efficient alternative. Instead of modifying the model’s internal parameters, soft prompting introduces learnable embeddings (soft prompts) that are prepended to the input sequence, enabling task adaptation with minimal computational cost. This approach is particularly appealing for tasks requiring minimal intervention in the model’s architecture while leveraging its pre-trained knowledge.

Despite the efficiency of soft prompting, its practical applicability faces challenges when dealing with black-box models where gradients with respect to the model parameters are inaccessible. For instance, many commercial APIs or proprietary models only provide access to predictions or loss values, making gradient-based optimization infeasible. In such scenarios, zeroth-order optimization becomes a crucial tool. Specifically, in this section, we consider a black-box, pre-trained language classifier fc:ℝLt×768→[0,1]f_{c}:\mathbb{R}^{L_{t}\times 768}\to[0,1], a pre-trained tokenizer ft:str→ℝLt×768f_{t}:\textup{str}\to\mathbb{R}^{L_{t}\times 768}, where str is any string of arbitrary length, and the sequence length LtL_{t} is a positive integer up to 512 representing the length of the embedding. The goal is to find a soft prompt 𝒙∗∈ℝ768\bm{x}^{\ast}\in\mathbb{R}^{768} such that

𝒙∗=arg​min𝐱⁡𝔼(𝐳,y)​[CE​(fc​(cat​[𝐱,ft​(𝐳)]),y)],\bm{x}^{\ast}=\argmin_{\bm{x}}\mathbb{E}_{(\bm{z},y)}\big[\textup{CE}(f_{c}(\textup{cat}[\bm{x},f_{t}(\bm{z})]),y)\big], (4.7)

where CE​(⋅,⋅)\textup{CE}(\cdot,\cdot) is the cross-entropy loss function, and the dataset (𝒛,y)∈str×{0,1}(\bm{z},y)\in\texttt{str}\times\{0,1\}. This particular formulation addresses a binary sentiment analysis task where a given string is classified as expressing a positive (11) or negative (00) sentiment. Since the classifier fcf_{c} is pre-trained and treated as a black box, gradient information for the loss function is unavailable, necessitating the use of zeroth-order optimization to solve the problem.

For the pre-trained classifier and tokenizer, we employed the BERT model, a state-of-the-art transformer-based architecture trained on large corpora. Specifically, we focused on a simplified version of BERT, named DistilBERT. Sentiment analysis on the aclImdb dataset was used as a soft prompting task. This dataset comprises movie reviews categorized into positive and negative sentiments, forming a binary classification problem. A D=768D=768 dimension soft prompt 𝒙\bm{x} is considered as the input. The transformer’s parameters were kept frozen to focus optimization on the soft prompt, reducing the degrees of freedom and computational overhead. For computational convenience, we focus on small-scale in this example. The HF model, as described in Equation (4.7), was evaluated using 10 samples from aclImdb to approximate the expectation, while the LF model leveraged only 2 samples that were randomly selected from them. Consequently, the evaluation cost ratio between HF and LF was 5:1.

We set the initial starting point at the origin. We let ℓ=50\ell=50, c=0.99c=0.99, and for the methods without line search we chose a fixed step size of 1×10−21\times 10^{-2}. The yy-axis in the following figure represents the average cross entropy loss. Figure 8 illustrates the performances of different competing methods with the BF-SSD demonstrating notable advantages.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we proposed and analyzed a bi-fidelity line search scheme designed to accelerate the convergence of zeroth-order optimization algorithms. By constructing a surrogate model using both computationally expensive high-fidelity (HF) and inexpensive low-fidelity (LF) objective function evaluations, our approach enables an efficient backtracking line search on the surrogate to determine suitable step sizes. This significantly reduces the reliance on costly HF evaluations, a common bottleneck in zeroth-order methods. We established theoretical convergence guarantees for this scheme under standard assumptions and subsequently integrated it into the stochastic subspace descent framework, yielding the Bi-Fidelity Stochastic Subspace Descent (BF-SSD) algorithm.

The practical efficacy of BF-SSD was demonstrated through comprehensive experiments across diverse applications, including a synthetic optimization benchmark, dual-form kernel ridge regression, black-box adversarial attacks, and the fine-tuning of transformer-based language models. Across these tasks, BF-SSD consistently outperformed relevant baseline methods, including standard gradient descent, coordinate descent, SPSA, and a purely high-fidelity SSD variant, particularly when comparing solution quality achieved for a given budget of HF evaluations.

These findings underscore the potential of leveraging bi-fidelity information within stochastic subspace methods to effectively address large-scale, high-dimensional optimization problems where function evaluations are expensive. While the current analysis focuses on deterministic subspace steps, future work could extend the theoretical guarantees to encompass the stochastic nature of gradient estimation within the SSD framework. Overall, BF-SSD presents a promising and computationally efficient optimization tool for a variety of challenging real-world applications.

Appendix A Proof of Lemma 2.7

Proof.

We let nkn_{k} evaluations positioned at equispaced points between 𝒙k\bm{x}_{k} and 𝒙k+αmax​𝒗k\bm{x}_{k}+\alpha_{\textup{max}}\bm{v}_{k}, each sub-interval has length αmax/nk\alpha_{\textup{max}}/n_{k}. We also define ψk​(α)≔φ⁡(α)−fLF​(𝒙+α​𝒗k)\psi_{k}(\alpha)\coloneqq\varphi(\alpha)-f^{\textup{LF}}(\bm{x}+\alpha\bm{v}_{k}). For each sub-interval, we define the surrogate ψ~k​(α,nk)\tilde{\psi}_{k}(\alpha;n_{k}) as a linear function connecting these values.

WLOG, we prove the bound in Equation (2.8) holds in the interval α∈[0,h]\alpha\in[0,h] with h=αmax/nkh=\alpha_{\textup{max}}/n_{k} and this result can be extended to other sub-intervals. The surrogate ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha) is defined as

ψ~k​(α,nk)≔h−αh​ψ​(0)+αh​ψ​(h),α∈[0,h],\tilde{\psi}_{k}(\alpha;n_{k})\coloneqq\frac{h-\alpha}{h}\psi(0)+\frac{\alpha}{h}\psi(h),\quad\alpha\in[0,h], (A.1)

and similar definitions of ψ~k​(α,nk)\tilde{\psi}_{k}(\alpha;n_{k}) hold when α\alpha in other sub-intervals. Such linear approximation ψ~k​(α)\tilde{\psi}_{k}(\alpha) satisfies

|φ⁡(α)−φ~k​(α,nk)|=|ψ⁡(α)−ψ~k​(α,nk)|=|h−αh​(ψ⁡(0)−ψ⁡(α))+αh​(ψ⁡(h)−ψ⁡(α))|,\lvert\varphi(\alpha)-\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(\alpha;n_{k})\rvert=|\psi(\alpha)-\tilde{\psi}_{k}(\alpha;n_{k})|=\bigg|\frac{h-\alpha}{h}\left(\psi(0)-\psi(\alpha)\right)+\frac{\alpha}{h}\left(\psi(h)-\psi(\alpha)\right)\bigg|, (A.2)

for any α∈[0,h]\alpha\in[0,h]. Since the Lipschitz constant of ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha) is strictly controlled by WW and the fact that 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k} is a unit vector, Equation (A.2) satisfies

|φ⁡(α)−φ~k​(α,nk)|≤W​αmax/nk−ααmax/nk​(α−0)+W​ααmax/nk​(αmax/nk−α)≤W​αmax2​nk,∀α∈[0,h].\lvert\varphi(\alpha)-\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(\alpha;n_{k})\rvert\leq W\frac{\alpha_{\textup{max}}/n_{k}-\alpha}{\alpha_{\textup{max}}/n_{k}}(\alpha-0)+W\frac{\alpha}{\alpha_{\textup{max}}/n_{k}}(\alpha_{\textup{max}}/n_{k}-\alpha)\leq\frac{W\alpha_{\textup{max}}}{2n_{k}},\quad\forall\alpha\in[0,h]. (A.3)

Since we have

nk≥W​L​(1+c)​αmaxc​β​∥𝒗k∥2,n_{k}\geq\frac{WL(1+c)\alpha_{\textup{max}}}{c\beta\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}}, (A.4)

the sup-norm is bounded as

|φ⁡(α)−φ~k​(α,nk)|≤c​β​∥𝒗k∥22​(1+c)​L=∥𝒗k∥22​min⁡{c(1+c)2​L,c​β(1+c)​L,β​αmax},\lvert\varphi(\alpha)-\tilde{\varphi}_{k}(\alpha;n_{k})\rvert\leq\frac{c\beta\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}}{2(1+c)L}=\frac{\lVert\bm{v}_{k}\rVert^{2}}{2}\min\left\{\frac{c}{(1+c)^{2}L},\frac{c\beta}{(1+c)L},\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}}\right\}, (A.5)

where the last equality stems from the fact that β≤1/2\beta\leq 1/2 and αmax≥c/(c​L+L)\alpha_{\textup{max}}\geq c/(cL+L). ∎

Appendix B Single-fidelity SSD with Line Search

B.1 Assuming Strong-convexity

Assumption B.1.

Assume the objective function fHFf^{\textup{HF}} and algorithm satisfies the following conditions

  1. 1.

    𝑷k∈ℝD×ℓ\bm{P}_{k}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D\times\ell} are independent random matrices such that 𝔼⁡[𝑷k​𝑷kT]=𝑰d\mathbb{E}[\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}]=\bm{I}_{d} and 𝑷kT​𝑷k=(D/ℓ)​𝑰ℓ\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\bm{P}_{k}=(D/\ell)\bm{I}_{\ell} with D>ℓD>\ell;

  2. 2.

    Objective function fHF:ℝD→ℝf^{\textup{HF}}:{\mathbb{R}}^{D}\to{\mathbb{R}} attains its minimum f∗f^{*} and ∇fHF\nabla f^{\textup{HF}} is LL-Lipschitz continuous;

  3. 3.

    Objective function fHF:ℝD→ℝf^{\textup{HF}}:{\mathbb{R}}^{D}\to{\mathbb{R}} is γ\gamma-strongly convex; note γ≤L\gamma\leq L.

Theorem B.2.

(Single fidelity) With the assumptions of B.1, SSD with line search (either exact line search or backtracking) converges in the sense that f⁡(𝐱k)​→a.s.​f∗f(\bm{x}_{k})\overset{a.s.}{\to}f^{*} and f⁡(𝐱k)​→L1​f∗f(\bm{x}_{k})\overset{L^{1}}{\to}f^{*}.

Proof.

Define the filtration ℱk≔σ⁡(𝑷1,…,𝑷k−1)\mathcal{F}_{k}\coloneqq\sigma(\bm{P}_{1},\dots,\bm{P}_{k-1}) and ℱ1={∅,Ω}\mathcal{F}_{1}=\{\emptyset,\Omega\}. By Lipschitz continuity, we have

f(𝒙k+1)≤f(𝒙k)+∇f(𝒙k)T(𝒙k+1−𝒙k)+L2∥𝒙k+1−𝒙k∥2.f(\bm{x}_{k+1})\leq f(\bm{x}_{k})+\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})^{T}(\bm{x}_{k+1}-\bm{x}_{k})+\frac{L}{2}\lVert\bm{x}_{k+1}-\bm{x}_{k}\rVert^{2}. (B.1)

By defining fe​(𝒙)≔f⁡(𝒙)−f∗f_{e}(\bm{x})\coloneqq f(\bm{x})-f^{*} and plugging 𝒙k+1=𝒙k−αk𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)\bm{x}_{k+1}=\bm{x}_{k}-\alpha_{k}\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}), Equation (B.1) yields

fe​(𝒙k+1)−fe​(𝒙k)\displaystyle f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})-f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k}) ≤−αk⟨∇f(𝒙k),𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)⟩+αk2​L2⟨𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k),𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)⟩\displaystyle\leq-\alpha_{k}\langle\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}),\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rangle+\frac{\alpha_{k}^{2}L}{2}\langle\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}),\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rangle (B.2)
=−αk⟨∇f(𝒙k),𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)⟩+D​αk2​L2​ℓ⟨∇f(𝒙k),𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)⟩\displaystyle=-\alpha_{k}\langle\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}),\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rangle+\frac{D\alpha_{k}^{2}L}{2\ell}\langle\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}),\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rangle
=(−αk+D​αk2​L2​ℓ)⟨∇f(𝒙k),𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)⟩,\displaystyle=\left(-\alpha_{k}+\frac{D\alpha_{k}^{2}L}{2\ell}\right)\langle\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}),\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rangle,

where the fact 𝑷k​𝑷kT​𝑷k​𝑷kT=(D/ℓ)​𝑷k​𝑷kT\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}=(D/\ell)\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T} is applied. We have two line search approaches to determine the step size αk\alpha_{k},

  1. 1.

    Exact line search:

    αk=arg​minαf(𝐱k−α𝐏k𝐏kT∇f(𝐱k));\alpha_{k}=\argmin_{\alpha}f(\bm{x}_{k}-\alpha\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})); (B.3)
  2. 2.

    Backtracking: for some fixed αmax>0\alpha_{\textup{max}}>0, β∈(0,ℓ/2​d)\beta\in(0,\ell/2d), and c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1),

    αk\displaystyle\alpha_{k} =maxm∈ℕ⁡cm​αmax\displaystyle=\max_{m\in\mathbb{N}}c^{m}\alpha_{\textup{max}} (B.4)
    s.t.f(𝒙k−cmαmax𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k))\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad f(\bm{x}_{k}-c^{m}\alpha_{\textup{max}}\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})) ≤f(𝒙k)−βcmαmax∥𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)∥2.\displaystyle\leq f(\bm{x}^{k})-\beta c^{m}\alpha_{\textup{max}}\lVert\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}^{k})\rVert^{2}.

We will prove the convergence for two line search methods separately. All the following analyses hold for any 𝑷k\bm{P}_{k} satisfying Assumption B.1.

Exact line search

According to Equation (B.3), the exact line search method can find the optimal αk\alpha_{k} such that the quadratic term in Equation (B.2) yields −αk+Dαk2L/2ℓ≤−ℓ/(2dL)-\alpha_{k}+D\alpha_{k}^{2}L/2\ell\leq-\ell/(2dL) for any 𝑷k\bm{P}_{k}, thereby

fe(𝒙k+1)−fe(𝒙k)≤−ℓ2​d​L⟨∇f(𝒙k),𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)⟩∀𝑷k.f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})-f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})\leq-\frac{\ell}{2dL}\langle\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}),\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rangle\quad\forall\bm{P}_{k}. (B.5)

With condition on the current filtration ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k}, the conditional expectation on both sides turn to

𝔼⁡[fe​(𝒙k+1)|ℱk]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})|\mathcal{F}_{k}] ≤−ℓ2​d​L𝔼[⟨∇f(𝒙k),𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)⟩|ℱk]+fe(𝒙k)\displaystyle\leq-\frac{\ell}{2dL}\mathbb{E}\left[\langle\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}),\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rangle|\mathcal{F}_{k}\right]+f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k}) (B.6)
=−ℓ2​d​L​∥∇f​(𝒙k)∥2+fe​(𝒙k),\displaystyle=-\frac{\ell}{2dL}\lVert\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2}+f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k}),

where the equality is from the fact 𝔼⁡[𝑷k​𝑷kT|ℱk]=𝑰d\mathbb{E}[\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}|\mathcal{F}_{k}]=\bm{I}_{d}. By invoking the Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality,

𝔼⁡[fe​(𝒙k+1)|ℱk]≤−γ​ℓD​L​fe​(𝒙k)+fe​(𝒙k)=(1−γ​ℓD​L)​fe​(𝒙k).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})|\mathcal{F}_{k}]\leq-\frac{\gamma\ell}{DL}f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})+f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})=\left(1-\frac{\gamma\ell}{DL}\right)f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k}). (B.7)

Recursive application yields

𝔼⁡[fe​(𝒙k+1)|ℱk]≤(1−γ​ℓD​L)​fe​(𝒙k)=(1−γ​ℓD​L)​𝔼​[fe​(𝒙k)|ℱk−1]≤(1−γ​ℓD​L)k+1​𝔼​[fe​(𝒙0)].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})|\mathcal{F}_{k}]\leq\left(1-\frac{\gamma\ell}{DL}\right)f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})=\left(1-\frac{\gamma\ell}{DL}\right)\mathbb{E}[f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})|\mathcal{F}_{k-1}]\leq\left(1-\frac{\gamma\ell}{DL}\right)^{k+1}\mathbb{E}[f_{e}(\bm{x}_{0})]. (B.8)

Since ℓ≤D\ell\leq D and γ≤L\gamma\leq L, the term 1−γ​ℓ/D​L1-\gamma\ell/DL is less than 11. Equation (B.8) implies

𝔼⁡[f⁡(𝒙k+1)]−f∗≤(1−γ​ℓD​L)k+1​𝔼​[(f⁡(𝒙0)−f∗)]=(1−γ​ℓD​L)k+1​(f⁡(𝒙0)−f∗),\mathbb{E}\left[f(\bm{x}_{k+1})\right]-f^{*}\leq\left(1-\frac{\gamma\ell}{DL}\right)^{k+1}\mathbb{E}[(f(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*})]=\left(1-\frac{\gamma\ell}{DL}\right)^{k+1}(f(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*}), (B.9)

which proves f⁡(𝒙k)​→a.s.​f∗f(\bm{x}_{k})\overset{a.s.}{\to}f^{*} and f⁡(𝒙k)​→L1​f∗f(\bm{x}_{k})\overset{L^{1}}{\to}f^{*}.

Backtracking

(Showing the existence of a feasible set such that the Armijo condition is satisfied.) Following Equation (B.4), the backtracking method selects the maximal possible step size value that satisfies the Armijo condition with specified parameter β≤ℓ/2​d\beta\leq\ell/2d and shrinking parameter c<1c<1. When 0≤αk≤ℓ/D​L0\leq\alpha_{k}\leq\ell/DL, −αk+Dαk2L/2ℓ≤−αk/2-\alpha_{k}+D\alpha_{k}^{2}L/2\ell\leq-\alpha_{k}/2 holds with Haar measure probability one, which implies the following Armijo stopping condition

f⁡(𝒙k+1)\displaystyle f(\bm{x}_{k+1}) ≤f(𝒙k)−αk⟨∇f(𝒙k),𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)⟩+D​αk2​L2​ℓ⟨∇f(𝒙k),𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)⟩\displaystyle\leq f(\bm{x}_{k})-\alpha_{k}\langle\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}),\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rangle+\frac{D\alpha_{k}^{2}L}{2\ell}\langle\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}),\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rangle (B.10)
≤f(𝒙k)−αk2⟨∇f(𝒙k),𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)⟩\displaystyle\leq f(\bm{x}_{k})-\frac{\alpha_{k}}{2}\langle\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}),\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rangle
=f(𝒙k)−αk​ℓ2​d∥𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)∥2\displaystyle=f(\bm{x}_{k})-\frac{\alpha_{k}\ell}{2d}\lVert\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2}
≤f(𝒙k)−βαk∥𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)∥2.\displaystyle\leq f(\bm{x}_{k})-\beta\alpha_{k}\lVert\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2}.

Therefore, the backtracking terminates when αk=αmax\alpha_{k}=\alpha_{\textup{max}} or αk≥ℓ​c/D​L\alpha_{k}\geq\ell c/DL, which implies

fe(𝒙k+1)≤fe(𝒙k)−βαmax⟨∇f(𝒙k),𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)⟩,f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})\leq f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})-\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}}\langle\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}),\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rangle, (B.11)

or

fe(𝒙k+1)≤fe(𝒙k)−ℓ​c​βD​L⟨∇f(𝒙k),𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)⟩.f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})\leq f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})-\frac{\ell c\beta}{DL}\langle\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}),\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rangle. (B.12)

Similar with Equation (B.6), by combining Equations (B.11) and (B.12), and taking expectations conditioned on the filtration ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k}, we have

𝔼⁡[fe​(𝒙k+1)|ℱk]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})|\mathcal{F}_{k}] ≤−min{βαmax,ℓ​c​βD​L}𝔼[⟨∇f(𝒙k),𝑷k𝑷kT∇f(𝒙k)⟩|ℱk]+fe(𝒙k)\displaystyle\leq-\min\left\{\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{\ell c\beta}{DL}\right\}\mathbb{E}\left[\langle\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k}),\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rangle|\mathcal{F}_{k}\right]+f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k}) (B.13)
=−min⁡{β​αmax,ℓ​c​βD​L}​∥∇f​(𝒙k)∥2+fe​(𝒙k).\displaystyle=-\min\left\{\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{\ell c\beta}{DL}\right\}\lVert\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2}+f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k}).

Similar to Equation (B.7), by invoking the Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality,

𝔼⁡[fe​(𝒙k+1)|ℱk]≤−min⁡{2​γ​β​αmax,2​ℓ​c​γ​βD​L}​fe​(𝒙k)+fe​(𝒙)=(1−min⁡{2​γ​β​αmax,2​ℓ​c​γ​βD​L})​fe​(𝒙k).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})|\mathcal{F}_{k}]\leq-\min\left\{2\gamma\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{2\ell c\gamma\beta}{DL}\right\}f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})+f_{e}(\bm{x})=\left(1-\min\left\{2\gamma\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{2\ell c\gamma\beta}{DL}\right\}\right)f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k}). (B.14)

By recursively implementing Equation (B.14), we have

𝔼⁡[fe​(𝒙k+1)]≤(1−min⁡{2​γ​β​αmax,2​ℓ​c​γ​βD​L})k+1​fe​(𝒙0).\mathbb{E}[f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})]\leq\left(1-\min\left\{2\gamma\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{2\ell c\gamma\beta}{DL}\right\}\right)^{k+1}f_{e}(\bm{x}_{0}). (B.15)

Since 0<c<00<c<0, 0<γ≤L0<\gamma\leq L, 0<ℓ≤D0<\ell\leq D, and 0<β<0.50<\beta<0.5, the term 0<(1−min⁡{2​γ​β,2​ℓ​c​γ​β/D​L})<10<\left(1-\min\{2\gamma\beta,2\ell c\gamma\beta/DL\}\right)<1, the convergences f⁡(𝒙k)​→a.s.​f∗f(\bm{x}_{k})\overset{a.s.}{\to}f^{*} and f⁡(𝒙k)​→L1​f∗f(\bm{x}_{k})\overset{L^{1}}{\to}f^{*} are guaranteed. ∎

B.2 Assuming Convexity

Assumption B.3.

For the non-strongly convex objective function fHFf^{\textup{HF}} and the algorithm, we make the following assumptions

  1. 1.

    𝑷k∈ℝD×ℓ\bm{P}_{k}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D\times\ell} are independent random matrices such that 𝔼⁡[𝑷k​𝑷kT]=𝑰d\mathbb{E}[\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}]=\bm{I}_{d} and 𝑷kT​𝑷k=(D/ℓ)​𝑰ℓ\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\bm{P}_{k}=(D/\ell)\bm{I}_{\ell} with D>ℓD>\ell;

  2. 2.

    Objective function fHF:ℝD→ℝf^{\textup{HF}}:{\mathbb{R}}^{D}\to{\mathbb{R}} is convex and ∇fHF\nabla f^{\textup{HF}} is LL-Lipschitz continuous;

  3. 3.

    The function fHFf^{\textup{HF}} attains its minimum(s) f∗f^{*} at x∗x^{*} so that there exists a known RR satisfying max𝒙,𝒙∗⁡{∥𝒙−𝒙∗∥:fHF​(𝒙)≤fHF​(𝒙0)}≤R\max_{\bm{x},\bm{x}^{*}}\{\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{x}^{*}\rVert:f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x})\leq f^{\textup{HF}}(\bm{x}_{0})\}\leq R;

Given the above convex-but-not-strongly-convex assumption, we have the following L1L^{1} convergence result:

Theorem B.4.

With backtracking implemented for line search, we have

𝔼⁡[f⁡(𝒙k)]−f∗≤max⁡{2​R2k​β​αmax,2​d​L​R2k​ℓ​c​β}.\mathbb{E}[f(\bm{x}_{k})]-f^{*}\leq\max\left\{\frac{2R^{2}}{k\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}}},\frac{2dLR^{2}}{k\ell c\beta}\right\}. (B.16)
Proof.

We use the same notation as in the proof of Thm. B.2. Starting from Equation (B.13), we have

𝔼⁡[fe​(𝒙k+1)|ℱk]=−min⁡{β​αmax,ℓ​c​βD​L}​∥∇f​(𝒙k)∥2+fe​(𝒙k).\mathbb{E}[f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})|\mathcal{F}_{k}]=-\min\left\{\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{\ell c\beta}{DL}\right\}\lVert\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2}+f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k}). (B.17)

By convexity and the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality, ∥∇f​(𝒙k)∥≥fe​(𝒙k)/R\lVert\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert\geq f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})/R. With the fact that 𝔼​fe​(𝒙k+1)≤𝔼​fe​(𝒙k)\mathbb{E}f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})\leq\mathbb{E}f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k}), we have

𝔼​fe​(𝒙k+1)−fe​(𝒙k)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})-f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k}) ≤−min⁡{β​αmax,ℓ​c​βD​L}​𝔼​fe2​(𝒙k)2​R2\displaystyle\leq-\min\left\{\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{\ell c\beta}{DL}\right\}\frac{\mathbb{E}f^{2}_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})}{2R^{2}} (B.18)
≤−min⁡{β​αmax,ℓ​c​βD​L}​𝔼2​fe​(𝒙k)2​R2\displaystyle\leq-\min\left\{\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{\ell c\beta}{DL}\right\}\frac{\mathbb{E}^{2}f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})}{2R^{2}}
≤−min⁡{β​αmax,ℓ​c​βD​L}​𝔼​fe​(𝒙k+1)​𝔼​fe​(𝒙k)2​R2,\displaystyle\leq-\min\left\{\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{\ell c\beta}{DL}\right\}\frac{\mathbb{E}f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})\mathbb{E}f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})}{2R^{2}},

which further implies

1𝔼​fe​(𝒙k+1)≥1𝔼​fe​(𝒙k)+2​R2​min⁡{β​αmax,ℓ​c​βD​L}.\frac{1}{\mathbb{E}f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})}\geq\frac{1}{\mathbb{E}f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})}+2R^{2}\min\left\{\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{\ell c\beta}{DL}\right\}. (B.19)

Applying (B.19) recursively, we obtain

𝔼​fe​(𝒙k+1)≤(min⁡{β​αmax,ℓ​c​βD​L})−1​2​R2k=max⁡{2​R2k​β​αmax,2​d​L​R2k​ℓ​c​β}.\mathbb{E}f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})\leq\left(\min\left\{\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{\ell c\beta}{DL}\right\}\right)^{-1}\frac{2R^{2}}{k}=\max\left\{\frac{2R^{2}}{k\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}}},\frac{2dLR^{2}}{k\ell c\beta}\right\}. (B.20)

∎

B.3 No convexity assumptions

Assumption B.5.

We make the following assumptions:

  1. 1.

    𝑷k∈ℝD×ℓ\bm{P}_{k}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D\times\ell} are independent random matrices such that 𝔼⁡[𝑷k​𝑷kT]=𝑰d\mathbb{E}[\bm{P}_{k}\bm{P}_{k}^{T}]=\bm{I}_{d} and 𝑷kT​𝑷k=(D/ℓ)​𝑰ℓ\bm{P}_{k}^{T}\bm{P}_{k}=(D/\ell)\bm{I}_{\ell} with D>ℓD>\ell;

  2. 2.

    The objective function fHF:ℝD→ℝf^{\textup{HF}}:{\mathbb{R}}^{D}\to{\mathbb{R}} (or fHFf^{\textup{HF}}) attains its minimum f∗f^{*} and ∇fHF\nabla f^{\textup{HF}} is LL-Lipschitz continuous;

When Assumption B.5 holds, we have the following L2L^{2} convergence of the gradient norm result for SSD with line search:

Theorem B.6.

With Assumption B.5 holding and backtracking implemented for line search, we have

mink∈{0,…,K}⁡𝔼⁡[∥∇f​(𝒙k)∥2]≤max⁡{(f⁡(𝒙0)−f∗)(K+1)​β​αmax,D​L​(f⁡(𝒙0)−f∗)(K+1)​ℓ​c​β}.\min_{k\in\{0,\dots,K\}}\mathbb{E}[\lVert\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2}]\leq\max\left\{\frac{(f(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*})}{(K+1)\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}}},\frac{DL(f(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*})}{(K+1)\ell c\beta}\right\}. (B.21)

That is, k=𝒪⁡(1/(ϵ​β​αmax)+D​L/(ϵ​ℓ​c​β))k=\mathcal{O}(1/(\epsilon\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}})+DL/(\epsilon\ell c\beta)) iterations are required to achieve 𝔼​∥∇f​(𝐱k)∥2≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\lVert\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2}\leq\epsilon.

Proof.

Following Equation (B.13)

min⁡{β​αmax,ℓ​c​βD​L}​∥∇f​(𝒙k)∥2≤fe​(𝒙k)−𝔼⁡[fe​(𝒙k+1)|ℱk],\min\left\{\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{\ell c\beta}{DL}\right\}\lVert\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2}\leq f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})-\mathbb{E}[f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})|\mathcal{F}_{k}], (B.22)

which leads to the telescope series

min⁡{β​αmax,ℓ​c​βD​L}​∑k=0K∥∇f​(𝒙k)∥2\displaystyle\min\left\{\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{\ell c\beta}{DL}\right\}\sum_{k=0}^{K}\lVert\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2} ≤∑k=0K(fe​(𝒙k)−𝔼⁡[fe​(𝒙k+1)|ℱk])\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{K}\left(f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k})-\mathbb{E}[f_{e}(\bm{x}_{k+1})|\mathcal{F}_{k}]\right) (B.23)
=f⁡(𝒙0)−𝔼​f​(𝒙K+1)≤f⁡(𝒙0)−f∗.\displaystyle=f(\bm{x}_{0})-\mathbb{E}f(\bm{x}_{K+1})\leq f(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*}.

Therefore,

(K+1)​mink∈{0,…,K}​𝔼​∥∇f​(𝒙k)∥2\displaystyle(K+1)\min_{k\in\{0,\dots,K\}}\mathbb{E}\lVert\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2} ≤(min⁡{β​αmax,ℓ​c​βD​L})−1​(f⁡(𝒙0)−f∗)\displaystyle\leq\left(\min\left\{\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}},\frac{\ell c\beta}{DL}\right\}\right)^{-1}(f(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*}) (B.24)
=max⁡{(f⁡(𝒙0)−f∗)β​αmax,D​L​(f⁡(𝒙0)−f∗)ℓ​c​β}.\displaystyle=\max\left\{\frac{(f(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*})}{\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}}},\frac{DL(f(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*})}{\ell c\beta}\right\}.

A sufficient condition to let 𝔼​∥∇f​(𝒙k)∥2\mathbb{E}\lVert\nabla f(\bm{x}_{k})\rVert^{2} be ϵ\epsilon-small is to let

k≥max⁡{(f⁡(𝒙0)−f∗)ϵ​β​αmax,D​L​(f⁡(𝒙0)−f∗)ϵ​ℓ​c​β}.k\geq\max\left\{\frac{(f(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*})}{\epsilon\beta\alpha_{\textup{max}}},\frac{DL(f(\bm{x}_{0})-f^{*})}{\epsilon\ell c\beta}\right\}. (B.25)
